questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.question_text: A 30-year-old man has well-demarcated erythematous plaques with silvery scale over the extensor surfaces of elbows and knees. Gentle scraping reveals pinpoint bleeding. What is this sign called and the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The Auspitz sign (pinpoint bleeding after scale removal due to suprapapillary thinning of the epidermis) is classic for psoriasis along with well-demarcated plaques over extensor surfaces. Nikolsky sign refers to skin sliding/blistering with lateral pressure, seen in pemphigus, not psoriasis. Darier sign is wheal formation on stroking a lesion in mastocytosis. Koebner phenomenon (new lesions at trauma sites) occurs in both psoriasis and lichen planus and is not specific. Pearl: nail pitting and oil-drop sign also support a psoriasis diagnosis.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.question_text: A middle-aged woman presents with intensely pruritic, violaceous, polygonal papules on the flexor wrists, along with white lacy striae on the buccal mucosa. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Lichen planus presents with the '6 Ps' (pruritic, purple, polygonal, planar, papules, plaques) typically on flexor surfaces, and Wickham striae (white lacy lines) on mucosal/cutaneous lesions are characteristic. Psoriasis classically affects extensor surfaces with silvery scale, not violaceous flexor papules. Pityriasis rosea presents with a herald patch followed by a 'Christmas tree' distribution of oval plaques, not Wickham striae. Discoid lupus erythematosus presents with scarring, photosensitive plaques, typically on the face. Pearl: lichen planus has been associated with hepatitis C infection.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.image_title: Clinical photograph of oral mucosa and trunk
key_findings: Flaccid bullae with positive Nikolsky sign
Painful oral mucosal erosions preceding skin lesions
Crusted erosions at sites of ruptured bullae
questions.question_text: A middle-aged patient presents with the findings shown, including painful mouth ulcers preceding skin blistering. Biopsy shows intraepidermal acantholysis. Which immunofluorescence pattern and antigen target are expected?

options.B: Linear IgG along the basement membrane against BP180
options.C: Granular IgA deposits at dermal papillae tips
options.D: Linear IgA along the basement membrane

questions.explanation: Pemphigus vulgaris is caused by IgG autoantibodies against desmoglein 3 (and often desmoglein 1), producing intercellular 'net-like' or 'fishnet' immunofluorescence and intraepidermal (suprabasal) acantholysis with a positive Nikolsky sign; oral lesions typically precede skin involvement. Linear IgG against BP180 is seen in bullous pemphigoid, which presents with tense bullae and a negative Nikolsky sign. Granular IgA at dermal papillae tips is characteristic of dermatitis herpetiformis. Linear IgA deposition characterizes linear IgA bullous dermatosis. Pearl: pemphigus vulgaris is potentially life-threatening due to loss of skin barrier function and risk of secondary infection.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.question_text: An elderly patient presents with tense, fluid-filled bullae on flexural areas without oral involvement, and a negative Nikolsky sign. Which layer of skin is the site of blister formation?
questions.explanation: Bullous pemphigoid results from autoantibodies against hemidesmosomal proteins BP180/BP230 at the dermo-epidermal junction, causing subepidermal blister formation that produces tense, intact bullae and a negative Nikolsky sign, in contrast to pemphigus vulgaris's intraepidermal, fragile blisters. Intraepidermal suprabasal splitting characterizes pemphigus vulgaris. Stratum corneum-level changes occur in conditions like staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome. Subcutaneous fat involvement occurs in panniculitis, not blistering disorders. Pearl: bullous pemphigoid typically affects elderly patients and has a better prognosis than pemphigus vulgaris.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.question_text: A young adult with chronic diarrhea and weight loss develops intensely pruritic grouped vesicles over the elbows, knees, and buttocks. Which systemic association and serologic test best confirm the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Dermatitis herpetiformis is strongly associated with celiac disease (gluten-sensitive enteropathy), and anti-tissue transglutaminase (and anti-endomysial) antibodies support the diagnosis, with skin biopsy showing granular IgA deposits at dermal papillae tips. Hepatitis C is associated with lichen planus and porphyria cutanea tarda, not dermatitis herpetiformis. IgA nephropathy and anti-BP180 are unrelated serologic markers for this condition. ANCA is associated with vasculitides, not dermatitis herpetiformis. Pearl: a strict gluten-free diet can resolve both the GI and cutaneous manifestations.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.question_text: A 6-month-old infant has itchy, erythematous, scaly patches on the cheeks and extensor surfaces, with a family history of asthma and allergic rhinitis. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Atopic dermatitis in infants classically affects the face and extensor surfaces (later shifting to flexural areas in older children), is intensely pruritic, and is part of the 'atopic triad' with asthma and allergic rhinitis, often with a strong family history. Seborrheic dermatitis in infants ('cradle cap') is typically greasy and non-pruritic, affecting the scalp. Contact dermatitis is localized to the area of allergen/irritant exposure. Psoriasis classically affects extensor surfaces in older children/adults with silvery scale, not this infantile facial pattern. Pearl: atopic dermatitis is associated with filaggrin gene mutations causing skin barrier dysfunction.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.question_text: A woman develops an itchy, vesicular rash in a linear streaky pattern on her forearm two days after gardening. Which immune mechanism underlies this reaction?
questions.explanation: Allergic contact dermatitis (e.g., from poison ivy/urushiol) is a Type IV, T-cell-mediated delayed hypersensitivity reaction, with onset typically 24-48 hours after exposure and a linear/streaky pattern reflecting contact with the plant. Type I hypersensitivity (IgE-mediated) causes immediate reactions like urticaria/anaphylaxis, not this delayed eczematous pattern. Type II hypersensitivity involves antibody-mediated cytotoxicity (e.g., hemolytic reactions), unrelated here. Type III hypersensitivity involves immune complex deposition (e.g., serum sickness), not contact dermatitis. Pearl: patch testing is used to identify the causative allergen in suspected allergic contact dermatitis.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.question_text: An HIV-positive man develops greasy, yellowish scaling over the scalp, eyebrows, and nasolabial folds. Which organism is implicated in the pathogenesis of this condition?
questions.explanation: Seborrheic dermatitis is associated with an inflammatory response to Malassezia (formerly Pityrosporum) yeast in sebum-rich areas (scalp, eyebrows, nasolabial folds), and is markedly more severe and common in HIV-positive patients. Trichophyton rubrum causes dermatophyte infections like tinea, not seborrheic dermatitis. Candida albicans causes candidiasis in moist intertriginous areas, a different pattern. Staphylococcus aureus is implicated in impetigo and folliculitis, not seborrheic dermatitis. Pearl: topical antifungals (ketoconazole) and mild topical steroids are first-line treatment for seborrheic dermatitis.

questions.subject: Dermatology
key_findings: Annular erythematous plaque with central clearing
Absence of pustules within the lesion
questions.question_text: A farmer presents with the ring-shaped lesion shown. KOH mount of skin scraping would most likely reveal which finding?

options.C: Short hyphae with spores ('spaghetti and meatballs')

questions.explanation: Tinea corporis is a dermatophyte infection (Trichophyton, Microsporum, Epidermophyton) producing an annular plaque with an active scaly border and central clearing; KOH examination reveals septate branching hyphae. Pseudohyphae with budding yeast are seen in Candida infections, which present differently (typically in moist intertriginous areas). 'Spaghetti and meatballs' appearance (short hyphae plus spores) is characteristic of tinea versicolor caused by Malassezia. Branching aseptate hyphae are characteristic of Mucor/Rhizopus (mucormycosis), a deep, invasive fungal infection, not superficial dermatophytosis. Pearl: tinea corporis is treated with topical antifungals; widespread or recalcitrant cases may require oral therapy.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.question_text: A young adult presents with multiple hypopigmented, finely scaling macules on the upper trunk that become more noticeable after sun exposure/tanning. Which organism and KOH finding is expected?
questions.explanation: Tinea (pityriasis) versicolor is caused by Malassezia furfur, producing hypopigmented or hyperpigmented finely scaling macules, classically on the trunk, with the characteristic 'spaghetti and meatballs' appearance of short hyphae and round spores on KOH preparation. Trichophyton rubrum causes tinea corporis/pedis/cruris with septate hyphae but not this yeast-hyphae combination. Candida albicans shows pseudohyphae and budding yeast in moist areas, not this trunk distribution. Microsporum canis is a zoophilic dermatophyte causing tinea capitis/corporis with ectothrix spore invasion of hair, unrelated to versicolor. Pearl: the hypopigmentation in tinea versicolor results from azelaic acid produced by the organism, which inhibits melanocyte tyrosinase.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.question_text: A patient presents with intensely pruritic papules and linear burrows in the finger webs, wrists, and genital area, worse at night. Which is the first-line treatment?
questions.explanation: Scabies, caused by Sarcoptes scabiei, presents with intensely pruritic burrows in finger webs, wrists, and genital areas, with nocturnal worsening due to mite activity, and is treated first-line with topical permethrin 5% applied to the whole body. Clotrimazole and fluconazole are antifungals, ineffective against mites. Mupirocin is a topical antibiotic for bacterial skin infections like impetigo, not scabies. Pearl: all household contacts should be treated simultaneously to prevent reinfestation, and crusted (Norwegian) scabies in immunocompromised patients requires oral ivermectin.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.question_text: A schoolchild presents with intense scalp itching and nits attached to hair shafts near the scalp. Which is the most appropriate first-line treatment?
questions.explanation: Pediculosis capitis (head lice) is treated first-line with topical permethrin 1%, applied to the scalp and hair, with nit removal using a fine-toothed comb. Oral itraconazole is an antifungal, not effective against lice. Topical betamethasone is a steroid that would not eradicate the infestation. Oral doxycycline is an antibiotic, irrelevant to lice treatment. Pearl: nits adherent to hair shafts (versus easily removed dandruff flakes) help distinguish pediculosis from other scalp conditions.

questions.subject: Dermatology
key_findings: Grouped vesicles on an erythematous base
questions.question_text: An elderly patient presents with the painful unilateral dermatomal rash shown, preceded by burning pain. Which virus and pathophysiologic mechanism explains this presentation?

options.A: Reactivation of latent varicella-zoster virus from dorsal root ganglia
options.B: Primary infection with herpes simplex virus type 1
options.C: Reactivation of Epstein-Barr virus from B lymphocytes

questions.explanation: Herpes zoster (shingles) results from reactivation of latent varicella-zoster virus residing in dorsal root ganglia since primary chickenpox infection, causing a painful, unilateral, dermatomal vesicular eruption, often preceded by prodromal neuralgia. Primary HSV-1 infection causes orolabial/genital herpes, not this dermatomal pattern. EBV reactivation is associated with conditions like hairy leukoplakia and certain lymphomas, not zoster. Primary VZV infection causes chickenpox (varicella), a generalized vesicular rash, not the localized dermatomal reactivation pattern. Pearl: early antiviral therapy (within 72 hours) reduces the risk of postherpetic neuralgia.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.question_text: A sexually active young adult presents with painful grouped vesicles on an erythematous base in the genital region, with recurrent episodes. Which test best confirms active viral infection?

options.A: PCR for HSV DNA from lesion swab

questions.explanation: PCR for HSV DNA is the most sensitive and specific test for confirming active genital herpes simplex virus infection from a lesion swab. VDRL/RPR are serologic tests for syphilis, not HSV. Tanzck smear can show multinucleated giant cells in HSV but is nonspecific and shows acantholytic cells in pemphigus rather than being diagnostic on its own; it is less sensitive than PCR. KOH preparation detects fungal elements, not viral infection. Pearl: recurrent genital HSV is most commonly caused by HSV-2, while HSV-1 more often causes orolabial disease, though overlap is increasingly common.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.question_text: A child presents with multiple dome-shaped, flesh-colored papules with central umbilication on the trunk. Which virus family causes this condition?
questions.explanation: Molluscum contagiosum is caused by a poxvirus, producing characteristic dome-shaped, umbilicated, flesh-colored papules, spread by direct contact or fomites, and is common in children and sexually active adults. Papillomavirus (HPV) causes warts, which present as rough, hyperkeratotic papules without umbilication. Herpesvirus causes vesicular lesions on an erythematous base, not umbilicated papules. Picornavirus causes conditions like hand-foot-mouth disease, presenting differently. Pearl: molluscum lesions can be treated with curettage, cryotherapy, or may resolve spontaneously over months.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.question_text: A teenager presents with multiple rough, hyperkeratotic papules over the dorsal hand with pinpoint black dots when pared. Which virus causes this lesion?
questions.explanation: Common warts (verruca vulgaris) are caused by human papillomavirus, presenting as hyperkeratotic papules with thrombosed capillaries appearing as black dots ('seed warts') when the surface is pared. Molluscum contagiosum causes umbilicated papules, a distinct morphology. Varicella-zoster virus causes vesicular eruptions, not hyperkeratotic papules. Coxsackievirus causes hand-foot-mouth disease with vesicles on the hands, feet, and mouth, a different presentation. Pearl: HPV types 6 and 11 cause genital warts (condyloma acuminata), while types 16 and 18 are oncogenic, associated with cervical and other cancers.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.question_text: A young child presents with honey-colored crusted erosions around the nose and mouth. Which organisms most commonly cause this condition?
questions.explanation: Impetigo is most commonly caused by Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus pyogenes, producing the classic honey-colored ('golden') crusted lesions around the face, especially in children. Pseudomonas aeruginosa causes conditions like hot tub folliculitis or ecthyma gangrenosum, not classic impetigo. Candida albicans causes intertriginous candidiasis, not crusted facial lesions. Mycobacterium leprae causes leprosy, an entirely distinct chronic granulomatous disease. Pearl: nonbullous impetigo (Strep/Staph) is distinguished from bullous impetigo (purely Staph, exfoliative toxin-mediated) which produces flaccid bullae.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.question_text: A patient presents with a sharply demarcated, raised, bright red, warm, tender plaque on the lower leg with fever. Which is the most likely diagnosis and layer of skin involved?

options.B: Cellulitis; deep dermis and subcutaneous tissue

questions.explanation: Erysipelas involves the superficial dermis and superficial lymphatics, producing a sharply demarcated, raised, bright red plaque, classically caused by Streptococcus pyogenes, in contrast to cellulitis which involves deeper dermis/subcutaneous tissue with poorly demarcated borders. Cellulitis presents with less sharply defined borders and deeper tissue involvement. Necrotizing fasciitis involves the fascia with severe pain disproportionate to exam findings and systemic toxicity, a surgical emergency. Folliculitis is limited to hair follicles, presenting as small pustules, not a diffuse plaque. Pearl: the sharp demarcation in erysipelas reflects the superficial lymphatic involvement, distinguishing it clinically from cellulitis.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.question_text: A diabetic patient presents with rapidly progressive leg pain out of proportion to physical findings, with crepitus, bullae, and systemic toxicity. Which is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.A: Emergency surgical debridement plus broad-spectrum IV antibiotics

questions.explanation: Necrotizing fasciitis is a surgical emergency requiring immediate, aggressive surgical debridement of necrotic tissue combined with broad-spectrum IV antibiotics (covering polymicrobial and Group A streptococcus/Clostridium), as delay significantly increases mortality. Oral antibiotics and outpatient management are inadequate given the rapid progression and risk of sepsis/death. Topical treatment alone does not address the deep fascial infection. Observation risks rapid deterioration and death; this is a time-critical surgical emergency. Pearl: pain out of proportion to exam findings, crepitus, and rapidly spreading erythema are red flags for necrotizing fasciitis.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.question_text: A patient started on lamotrigine two weeks ago develops fever, painful mucosal erosions, and widespread epidermal detachment involving 35% of body surface area with a positive Nikolsky sign. Which is the diagnosis based on body surface area involved?
questions.explanation: Toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN) is defined by epidermal detachment involving more than 30% of body surface area, while Stevens-Johnson syndrome involves less than 10%, and SJS/TEN overlap involves 10-30%; both are severe drug reactions often triggered by anticonvulsants (lamotrigine), sulfonamides, and allopurinol. Stevens-Johnson syndrome would be the diagnosis if BSA involvement were under 10%, not 35%. Erythema multiforme is typically a milder, self-limited condition often triggered by HSV, with targetoid lesions and minimal mucosal involvement. Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome occurs in children due to exfoliative toxin and is not drug-induced. Pearl: SCORTEN scoring helps predict mortality risk in TEN.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.question_text: A young adult develops recurrent target-shaped lesions with a dusky center, dull red middle ring, and pale outer ring on the extremities one week after a cold sore outbreak. What is the most common trigger for this recurrent condition?
questions.explanation: Erythema multiforme presents with classic targetoid lesions and is most commonly triggered by herpes simplex virus infection, especially in recurrent cases, while drug reactions are a less common trigger for EM compared to SJS/TEN. Mycoplasma pneumoniae is more classically associated with Stevens-Johnson syndrome (sometimes called Mycoplasma-induced rash and mucositis). Sulfonamides and allopurinol are classic triggers for SJS/TEN, not the recurrent HSV-associated form of erythema multiforme. Pearl: recurrent erythema multiforme associated with HSV may benefit from prophylactic antiviral therapy.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.question_text: A patient develops transient, pruritic, erythematous wheals that blanch with pressure and resolve within 24 hours, recurring over several weeks. Which is the primary mediator responsible?
questions.explanation: Urticaria results from mast cell degranulation releasing histamine and other mediators, causing transient, pruritic, blanching wheals that classically resolve within 24 hours (individual lesions), distinguishing it from urticarial vasculitis where lesions persist longer and may not blanch. Complement-mediated cell lysis describes Type II hypersensitivity mechanisms, unrelated to typical urticaria. IgA immune complex deposition is seen in conditions like Henoch-Schönlein purpura, not typical urticaria. Direct bacterial toxin effects describe conditions like toxic shock or scalded skin syndrome, not urticaria. Pearl: chronic urticaria is defined as lasting more than 6 weeks and often requires evaluation for underlying autoimmune or other causes.

questions.subject: Dermatology
key_findings: Symmetric distribution over the dorsal hands
No surface scale or textural change
Lesions enhanced under Wood's lamp examination
questions.question_text: A young patient with the hand findings shown also has a history of autoimmune thyroiditis. Which underlying pathophysiologic process is responsible for this skin condition?

options.B: Reduced tyrosinase enzyme activity from birth

questions.explanation: Vitiligo results from autoimmune destruction of melanocytes, often associated with other autoimmune conditions such as autoimmune thyroiditis, type 1 diabetes, and pernicious anemia, producing sharply demarcated depigmented (not hypopigmented) macules. Reduced tyrosinase activity from birth describes albinism, a congenital condition rather than acquired autoimmune depigmentation. Post-inflammatory hypopigmentation follows a preceding inflammatory skin condition and is typically less sharply demarcated and partial, not complete depigmentation. Fungal-mediated pigment changes describe tinea versicolor, a distinct entity. Pearl: vitiligo lesions fluoresce brightly under Wood's lamp due to the complete absence of melanin.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.question_text: A pregnant woman develops symmetric brown patches on the cheeks and forehead that worsen with sun exposure. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Melasma presents as symmetric hyperpigmented patches on sun-exposed facial areas, strongly associated with pregnancy ('mask of pregnancy'), oral contraceptive use, and sun exposure, due to hormonally-stimulated melanocyte activity. Vitiligo causes depigmentation, the opposite finding. Tinea versicolor causes hypo- or hyperpigmented scaly macules on the trunk, not this facial distribution. Post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation follows a preceding inflammatory skin lesion at that specific site, not this hormonally-driven symmetric facial pattern. Pearl: strict photoprotection is essential in melasma management, as sun exposure significantly worsens pigmentation.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.question_text: A newborn has white hair, pale skin, photophobia, and nystagmus, with a normal number of melanocytes on biopsy. Which enzyme defect best explains this?
questions.explanation: Albinism results from tyrosinase deficiency or dysfunction, impairing melanin synthesis despite a normal number of melanocytes being present, causing generalized hypopigmentation of skin, hair, and eyes along with ocular findings like nystagmus and photophobia due to foveal hypoplasia. Tyrosine hydroxylase deficiency affects catecholamine synthesis, unrelated to pigmentation. Homogentisate oxidase deficiency causes alkaptonuria, a tyrosine degradation disorder unrelated to pigmentation. Phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency causes PKU, which can cause mild hypopigmentation but not classic albinism. Pearl: albinism increases the risk of skin cancers due to loss of melanin's UV-protective function.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.question_text: An obese teenager presents with velvety, hyperpigmented thickening of the skin in the axillae and posterior neck. Which underlying condition is most strongly associated?
questions.explanation: Acanthosis nigricans in the setting of obesity is most commonly associated with insulin resistance, where hyperinsulinemia stimulates keratinocyte and fibroblast proliferation via insulin-like growth factor receptors, producing velvety hyperpigmented plaques in flexural areas. Vitamin A deficiency causes xerosis and night blindness, not this finding. Hypothyroidism can cause dry, coarse skin but not this characteristic flexural hyperpigmentation pattern. Iron deficiency anemia causes pallor and koilonychia, not acanthosis nigricans. Pearl: sudden-onset acanthosis nigricans in an older, non-obese adult should raise suspicion for an underlying malignancy (gastric adenocarcinoma).

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.question_text: A teenager presents with comedones, papules, and pustules on the face. Which organism plays a key role in the inflammatory pathogenesis of this condition?
questions.explanation: Acne vulgaris pathogenesis involves follicular hyperkeratinization, increased sebum production, and proliferation of Cutibacterium (formerly Propionibacterium) acnes, which triggers an inflammatory response leading to papules and pustules. Staphylococcus epidermidis is a normal skin commensal not centrally implicated in acne pathogenesis. Malassezia furfur causes seborrheic dermatitis and tinea versicolor, not acne. Demodex folliculorum is implicated in rosacea and demodicosis, not classic acne vulgaris. Pearl: comedones (open and closed) are the primary, non-inflammatory lesions of acne, distinguishing it from purely inflammatory conditions like rosacea.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.question_text: A middle-aged woman presents with facial flushing, telangiectasias, and papulopustules over the central face, without comedones, worsened by alcohol and spicy food. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Rosacea presents with central facial erythema, flushing, telangiectasias, and papulopustules without comedones, often triggered by alcohol, spicy food, heat, and sun exposure, distinguishing it from acne vulgaris which features comedones. Acne vulgaris is characterized by comedones, which are absent in rosacea by definition. Seborrheic dermatitis presents with greasy scaling rather than flushing and telangiectasia. Systemic lupus erythematosus can cause a malar rash but typically spares the nasolabial folds and lacks pustules/telangiectasia in this pattern. Pearl: rhinophyma (nasal skin thickening) is a severe, late complication of untreated rosacea.

questions.subject: Dermatology
key_findings: Well-circumscribed round patch of complete hair loss
Normal hair density in surrounding areas
questions.question_text: A young adult presents with the sudden-onset scalp patch shown. Which underlying pathophysiologic mechanism is responsible for this non-scarring hair loss?

options.A: Autoimmune T-cell attack on hair follicles
options.C: Fungal invasion of the hair shaft

questions.explanation: Alopecia areata results from autoimmune T-cell-mediated attack on hair follicles, producing well-demarcated, non-scarring patches of hair loss with characteristic exclamation-point hairs at the margins, and is associated with other autoimmune conditions. Androgen-mediated miniaturization describes androgenetic alopecia, a diffuse, patterned process rather than discrete patches. Fungal invasion describes tinea capitis, which typically shows scaling and broken hair shafts, not smooth bald patches. Traction-induced damage describes traction alopecia, related to hairstyling practices rather than autoimmune attack. Pearl: alopecia totalis (complete scalp hair loss) and alopecia universalis (all body hair loss) represent severe variants of alopecia areata.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.question_text: A man in his 30s notices gradual bitemporal recession and vertex thinning of scalp hair. Which enzyme converts testosterone to the androgen most responsible for this process?
questions.explanation: Androgenetic alopecia is driven by dihydrotestosterone (DHT), produced from testosterone by 5-alpha-reductase, causing progressive follicular miniaturization in genetically susceptible hair follicles, producing the classic bitemporal and vertex thinning pattern; finasteride (a 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor) is used in treatment. Aromatase converts androgens to estrogens, the opposite pathway. 17-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase is involved in sex steroid interconversion but is not the key target enzyme in male pattern baldness treatment. 21-hydroxylase is involved in adrenal steroidogenesis (cortisol/aldosterone pathway), unrelated to this condition. Pearl: minoxidil (a vasodilator) and finasteride are the two main FDA-approved treatments for androgenetic alopecia.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.question_text: A postmenopausal woman presents with intense vulvar pruritus and white, atrophic, 'cigarette paper' plaques with associated architectural distortion of the labia. What is the most significant long-term complication to monitor for?
questions.explanation: Lichen sclerosus causes white, atrophic ('cigarette paper') plaques with architectural distortion, most commonly in the anogenital region of postmenopausal women, and carries an increased risk of vulvar squamous cell carcinoma, necessitating long-term monitoring and biopsy of any suspicious areas. Basal cell carcinoma is not the classic malignancy associated with lichen sclerosus. Melanoma is not specifically linked to lichen sclerosus in this manner. Kaposi sarcoma is associated with HHV-8 and immunosuppression (notably HIV), unrelated to lichen sclerosus. Pearl: potent topical corticosteroids are first-line therapy for lichen sclerosus, both for symptom control and to potentially reduce malignancy risk.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.question_text: A patient with ulcerative colitis develops a rapidly enlarging, painful ulcer with violaceous undermined borders on the leg. Which is the most likely diagnosis, and what characteristic feature should be avoided due to risk of worsening?
questions.explanation: Pyoderma gangrenosum is a neutrophilic dermatosis associated with inflammatory bowel disease, presenting as a rapidly progressive, painful ulcer with violaceous, undermined borders; it exhibits pathergy (worsening with trauma/surgical intervention), so aggressive debridement should generally be avoided in favor of immunosuppressive therapy. Necrotizing fasciitis is a distinct surgical emergency requiring urgent debridement, unlike PG where surgery can worsen the lesion. Venous ulcers occur in the setting of venous insufficiency with different morphology (gaiter area, less violaceous undermining) and respond to compression. Diabetic foot ulcers occur in the setting of neuropathy/vascular disease at pressure points, not this violaceous undermined morphology. Pearl: pyoderma gangrenosum is a diagnosis of exclusion, and biopsy mainly serves to rule out other causes of ulceration.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.question_text: A young woman presents with tender, erythematous nodules on the bilateral anterior shins along with bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy on chest X-ray. Which is the most likely underlying diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Erythema nodosum (a septal panniculitis) presenting with bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy is classically associated with sarcoidosis (Löfgren syndrome: erythema nodosum, bilateral hilar adenopathy, and arthralgias/fever). While tuberculosis, streptococcal infection, and pregnancy can all also trigger erythema nodosum, the combination with bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy specifically points toward sarcoidosis as the most likely cause in this vignette. Streptococcal pharyngitis is a common trigger of EN but would not explain hilar adenopathy. Pregnancy is a recognized trigger but similarly does not explain the chest X-ray finding. Pearl: erythema nodosum is a panniculitis (inflammation of subcutaneous fat), not a true vasculitis.

questions.subject: Dermatology
key_findings: Follicular plugging visible on close inspection
Distribution on sun-exposed face and scalp
questions.question_text: A young woman presents with the chronic facial plaques shown, which leave scarring and permanent hair loss where they involve the scalp. What proportion of patients with this localized skin disease will progress to systemic lupus erythematosus?
questions.explanation: Discoid lupus erythematosus is the most common form of chronic cutaneous lupus, producing scarring, atrophic, dyspigmented plaques with follicular plugging on sun-exposed areas; only a minority of patients (roughly 5-10%) progress to systemic lupus erythematosus, though ANA testing and monitoring are still recommended. The majority of DLE patients do not develop SLE, distinguishing it from acute cutaneous lupus, which has stronger systemic associations. Saying essentially all or none ever both misrepresent the established minority-progression rate. Pearl: DLE lesions cause permanent scarring alopecia when they involve the scalp, unlike the non-scarring alopecia seen in active SLE.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.question_text: A woman presents with Raynaud phenomenon, skin tightening of the fingers, telangiectasias, and dysphagia. Which autoantibody is most specific for the limited cutaneous form (CREST syndrome) of this disease?
questions.explanation: Anti-centromere antibodies are most specific for limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis (CREST syndrome: Calcinosis, Raynaud, Esophageal dysmotility, Sclerodactyly, Telangiectasia), which has a relatively better prognosis with less risk of early severe internal organ involvement compared to diffuse disease. Anti-Scl-70 (anti-topoisomerase I) is associated with diffuse systemic sclerosis, which carries higher risk of pulmonary fibrosis and rapid skin progression. Anti-Smith antibody is specific for systemic lupus erythematosus. Anti-Jo-1 antibody is associated with antisynthetase syndrome in dermatomyositis/polymyositis. Pearl: limited cutaneous disease has higher risk of pulmonary arterial hypertension, while diffuse disease has higher risk of pulmonary fibrosis and renal crisis.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.question_text: A middle-aged woman presents with proximal muscle weakness, a violaceous rash over the upper eyelids, and scaly erythematous papules over the knuckles. Which terms describe these two classic skin findings respectively?
questions.explanation: Dermatomyositis presents with the heliotrope rash (violaceous periorbital edema/erythema) and Gottron papules (scaly erythematous papules over the knuckles/extensor joints), alongside proximal muscle weakness from inflammatory myopathy. Malar rash and discoid lesions are characteristic of lupus erythematosus, not dermatomyositis. Livedo reticularis and digital infarcts are seen in vasculitic/vasculopathic conditions like antiphospholipid syndrome. Sclerodactyly and calcinosis cutis are features of systemic sclerosis/CREST syndrome. Pearl: dermatomyositis in adults, especially with new onset, warrants malignancy screening due to its paraneoplastic association.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.question_text: An elderly farmer presents with the slowly growing nasal lesion shown. Which feature best distinguishes this tumor's biological behavior from squamous cell carcinoma?

options.A: Very low metastatic potential despite local invasiveness
options.C: Rapid doubling time with hematogenous spread

questions.explanation: Basal cell carcinoma is the most common skin cancer, characterized by pearly papules with rolled borders, telangiectasias, and central ulceration, and despite being locally invasive ('rodent ulcer'), it has very low metastatic potential, unlike squamous cell carcinoma which has a higher (though still relatively low) risk of metastasis, especially in high-risk locations. Frequent early lymph node metastasis is more characteristic of more aggressive cancers, not classic BCC. Rapid doubling time with hematogenous spread does not characterize BCC's typically slow, locally invasive growth pattern. HPV association is more relevant to certain squamous cell carcinomas (e.g., genital, periungual) rather than BCC. Pearl: chronic sun exposure and basal cell nevus syndrome (Gorlin syndrome, PTCH1 mutation) are key risk factors for BCC.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.question_text: A renal transplant recipient on chronic immunosuppression develops a hyperkeratotic, ulcerated nodule on sun-exposed skin that grows rapidly over weeks. Which factor most increases this patient's risk for this skin cancer relative to the general population?
questions.explanation: Chronic immunosuppression (as in organ transplant recipients) markedly increases the risk of squamous cell carcinoma, which can behave more aggressively in this population with higher rates of recurrence and metastasis. Female sex is not a major risk factor; SCC is actually more common in men due to cumulative sun exposure patterns. Dark skin pigmentation is protective against UV-induced skin cancers due to higher melanin content. Younger age is not a risk factor; SCC incidence increases with age due to cumulative UV exposure. Pearl: SCC arising from actinic keratosis or in immunosuppressed patients carries a higher risk of metastasis than de novo SCC in immunocompetent individuals.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.image_title: Dermoscopic photograph of a pigmented lesion
key_findings: Variegated color including black, brown, and red areas
Recent change in size noted by the patient
questions.question_text: A fair-skinned patient presents with the pigmented lesion shown, which has changed over the past 3 months. Which single histologic factor is the most important prognostic determinant for this tumor?
questions.explanation: Melanoma prognosis is most strongly determined by Breslow depth (tumor thickness/depth of invasion), which correlates directly with risk of metastasis and overall survival, and forms the basis of staging and sentinel lymph node biopsy decisions. While ABCDE features (Asymmetry, Border irregularity, Color variation, Diameter, Evolution) help with clinical detection, they are not the primary prognostic determinant once a diagnosis is made. Presence of a pre-existing nevus does not determine prognosis once melanoma develops. Patient age can influence outcomes but is not the primary histologic prognostic factor. Pearl: melanoma is the deadliest skin cancer despite being less common than BCC/SCC, due to its higher metastatic potential.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.question_text: An elderly man with significant sun exposure has multiple rough, scaly, erythematous papules on the scalp and forearms. Into which malignancy can these lesions progress if untreated?
questions.explanation: Actinic keratosis is a premalignant lesion caused by chronic UV exposure, with a small but real risk of progression to squamous cell carcinoma, presenting as rough, scaly, erythematous papules on sun-exposed skin ('sandpaper' texture). It is not typically considered a direct precursor to basal cell carcinoma, which usually arises de novo. Melanoma's precursor lesions are typically atypical/dysplastic nevi, not actinic keratosis. Merkel cell carcinoma is a rare, aggressive neuroendocrine skin cancer not classically arising from actinic keratosis. Pearl: cryotherapy, topical 5-fluorouracil, and photodynamic therapy are common treatments for actinic keratosis.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.question_text: An elderly patient has multiple well-demarcated, 'stuck-on' appearing, brown-black papules on the trunk with a waxy surface. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Seborrheic keratosis is a common, benign epidermal lesion in older adults, presenting with a characteristic 'stuck-on,' waxy, well-demarcated appearance, and does not carry malignant potential. Melanoma typically shows the irregular ABCDE features and growth pattern, not this stuck-on benign morphology. Actinic keratosis is rough/scaly with malignant potential, distinct from the waxy benign appearance of seborrheic keratosis. Basal cell carcinoma presents as a pearly papule with telangiectasias, not a waxy stuck-on lesion. Pearl: sudden eruption of multiple seborrheic keratoses (sign of Leser-Trélat) can rarely indicate an internal malignancy.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.question_text: An elderly patient has chronic, scaly, erythematous patches that have slowly progressed to plaques over years, with biopsy showing atypical lymphocytes infiltrating the epidermis in small clusters. Which cell type characterizes this cutaneous T-cell lymphoma?

options.A: CD4+ T-helper cells forming Pautrier microabscesses

questions.explanation: Mycosis fungoides is the most common cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, characterized by malignant CD4+ T-helper cells infiltrating the epidermis, forming characteristic clusters called Pautrier microabscesses, with disease progressing slowly from patches to plaques to tumors over years. CD8+ cytotoxic T-cell predominance is not the classic immunophenotype of mycosis fungoides. B-lymphocyte proliferations characterize cutaneous B-cell lymphomas, a distinct category. Natural killer cell lymphomas are rare and have a different, often more aggressive, clinical course. Pearl: Sézary syndrome is the leukemic variant of mycosis fungoides, with circulating malignant T-cells (Sézary cells) and erythroderma.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.question_text: An HIV-positive patient with a low CD4 count develops multiple violaceous, non-blanching plaques and nodules on the skin and oral mucosa. Which virus is causally implicated in this malignancy?
questions.explanation: Kaposi sarcoma is caused by human herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8), and develops particularly in immunosuppressed patients (HIV/AIDS, transplant recipients), presenting as violaceous, non-blanching vascular plaques/nodules on skin and mucosa. HPV causes warts and is associated with cervical and some squamous cell cancers, not Kaposi sarcoma. EBV is associated with conditions like nasopharyngeal carcinoma, Burkitt lymphoma, and hairy leukoplakia, not Kaposi sarcoma. HIV itself creates the immunosuppressed environment permitting HHV-8 reactivation but is not the direct oncogenic agent. Pearl: improvement of immune status with antiretroviral therapy can lead to regression of HIV-associated Kaposi sarcoma.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.question_text: A child has six or more light brown patches on the trunk, axillary freckling, and multiple soft subcutaneous nodules. Which gene mutation underlies this autosomal dominant disorder?
questions.explanation: Neurofibromatosis type 1 results from NF1 gene mutations (encoding neurofibromin, a tumor suppressor), presenting with café-au-lait macules, axillary/inguinal freckling, neurofibromas, and Lisch nodules of the iris. TSC1/TSC2 mutations cause tuberous sclerosis, presenting with ash-leaf spots and facial angiofibromas, a different phenotype. PTCH1 mutations cause basal cell nevus (Gorlin) syndrome with multiple BCCs and jaw cysts. FBN1 mutations cause Marfan syndrome, a connective tissue disorder, not this pigmentary/neural tumor syndrome. Pearl: NF1 patients require monitoring for optic gliomas and other CNS tumors, as well as malignant transformation of plexiform neurofibromas.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.question_text: An infant with infantile spasms is found to have hypopigmented macules on the trunk that fluoresce under Wood's lamp, along with facial angiofibromas later in childhood. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Tuberous sclerosis complex presents with hypopigmented ash-leaf macules (best visualized under Wood's lamp), facial angiofibromas, seizures (including infantile spasms), and intracranial cortical tubers/subependymal nodules, due to TSC1/TSC2 mutations affecting the mTOR pathway. Neurofibromatosis type 1 presents with hyperpigmented (not hypopigmented) café-au-lait macules and neurofibromas, a different pigmentary pattern. Sturge-Weber syndrome presents with a facial port-wine stain and leptomeningeal angiomatosis, not ash-leaf macules. Incontinentia pigmenti presents with a characteristic blistering-to-pigmented streak progression in female infants, a distinct entity. Pearl: cardiac rhabdomyomas and renal angiomyolipomas are important extracutaneous manifestations of tuberous sclerosis.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.question_text: A child develops severe sunburn after minimal sun exposure, progressive skin freckling, and multiple skin cancers by age 10. Which DNA repair defect underlies this condition?

options.A: Defective nucleotide excision repair of UV-induced DNA damage

questions.explanation: Xeroderma pigmentosum results from defective nucleotide excision repair, impairing removal of UV-induced pyrimidine dimers, leading to extreme photosensitivity, premature skin aging, and a markedly elevated risk of skin cancers at a young age. Defective mismatch repair causes Lynch syndrome with colorectal/endometrial cancer predisposition, not this photosensitivity syndrome. Defective homologous recombination repair is associated with BRCA1/2-related cancer syndromes, unrelated to UV sensitivity. Defective base excision repair is linked to conditions like MUTYH-associated polyposis, not xeroderma pigmentosum. Pearl: strict UV avoidance, including specialized clothing and window films, is essential lifelong management for XP patients.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.question_text: A man with chronic alcohol use and hepatitis C develops blistering and skin fragility on the dorsal hands after sun exposure, along with hyperpigmentation and hypertrichosis. Which enzyme deficiency is responsible?
questions.explanation: Porphyria cutanea tarda, the most common porphyria, results from uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase deficiency (often acquired/unmasked by alcohol, hepatitis C, estrogen, or iron overload), causing photosensitive blistering, skin fragility, hyperpigmentation, and hypertrichosis, particularly on sun-exposed areas like the hands. Ferrochelatase deficiency causes erythropoietic protoporphyria, which presents with acute painful photosensitivity rather than blistering fragility. Porphobilinogen deaminase deficiency causes acute intermittent porphyria, which lacks cutaneous photosensitivity entirely. ALA synthase overactivity is a feature seen in several porphyrias but is not itself the defining enzymatic deficiency of PCT. Pearl: phlebotomy and avoidance of triggers (alcohol, estrogen) are mainstays of PCT management alongside antimalarials in select cases.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.question_text: A patient develops a well-demarcated, dusky red-violet patch at the same site on the genital skin each time he takes co-trimoxazole, leaving residual hyperpigmentation. What is this reaction pattern called?
questions.explanation: Fixed drug eruption presents as a well-demarcated, dusky red-violet to brown patch or plaque that recurs at the exact same site with re-exposure to the offending drug (classically sulfonamides, NSAIDs, tetracyclines), leaving residual hyperpigmentation. Stevens-Johnson syndrome involves widespread mucocutaneous involvement with systemic symptoms, not a single recurrent localized patch. Morbilliform drug eruption presents as a diffuse measles-like maculopapular rash, not a fixed localized lesion. DRESS syndrome involves systemic features (fever, eosinophilia, organ involvement) with a more diffuse rash, distinct from fixed drug eruption. Pearl: fixed drug eruption recurring on the glans penis is a classically tested presentation, often due to sulfonamides.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.question_text: A patient presents with a single, well-defined hypopigmented anesthetic skin patch and a thickened peripheral nerve, with a strong cell-mediated immune response and few bacilli on skin smear. Which form of leprosy does this represent?
questions.explanation: Tuberculoid leprosy occurs in patients with a strong cell-mediated (Th1) immune response, resulting in few, well-defined hypopigmented anesthetic patches, thickened nerves, and a paucibacillary picture (few bacilli on smear) due to effective bacterial containment. Lepromatous leprosy occurs with a weak cell-mediated response, producing numerous, poorly-defined lesions with diffuse infiltration and a multibacillary picture, the opposite pattern. Borderline lepromatous leprosy falls along the spectrum but more closely resembles the lepromatous, multibacillary end with less distinct, more numerous lesions. Indeterminate leprosy is an early, nonspecific stage prior to full polarization into either type. Pearl: lepromatous leprosy patients are more contagious due to high bacillary load, while tuberculoid disease is less contagious due to robust immune containment.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.question_text: A child develops palpable purpura on the lower extremities and buttocks, abdominal pain, arthralgia, and hematuria following an upper respiratory infection. Which immunoglobulin mediates the vascular deposition in this condition?
questions.explanation: Henoch-Schönlein purpura (IgA vasculitis) is a small-vessel vasculitis mediated by IgA immune complex deposition in vessel walls, presenting with the classic tetrad of palpable purpura, arthralgia, abdominal pain, and renal involvement (hematuria), often following an upper respiratory infection in children. IgE-mediated mechanisms underlie Type I hypersensitivity reactions like urticaria/anaphylaxis, not this vasculitis. IgM is involved in early immune responses and some autoimmune cytopenias, not the defining mechanism here. IgG alone, without the characteristic IgA predominance, does not capture the specific immunopathology of this disease. Pearl: HSP nephritis shares pathologic similarities with IgA nephropathy (Berger disease), representing a systemic versus renal-limited spectrum of the same underlying IgA-mediated process.
